title: Crime College: What Prison Really Teaches
author: Emmett Tatter
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/emiliano-bar-
PaKHbtTDqt0-unsplash-1-680x452.jpg)

Image by Emiliano Bar.

A friend once said to me, "Prison seems like a crime college for some and a
complete waste of time for others. It doesn't rehabilitate people in ways that
a year or two in a mental health program or house arrest couldn't do better.
Mostly, it feels like a warehouse system that lets the wealthy and connected
bilk tax dollars in the name of fighting crime."

This is my answer.

When I hear "complete waste of time," I'm talking about what I saw day in and
day out. Men sat on racks, staring at concrete walls and bars surrounded by
chaos, waiting on count time, chow, and mail that never comes. Guys shuffled
through bullshit "anger management" and "thinking errors" classes taught by
people who'd rather be someplace else, then walked back to the dorm to find
the same violence, the same K-2 smoke, the same corrupt staff. Nothing changed
except the scars. We served the time. The time didn't serve us.

I went in at twenty-one, facing a life sentence, and ended up serving a ten-
year mandatory sentence in the Florida Department of Corrections.
"Corrections," yeah right. By twenty-two, my first job inside the DOC was
wrapping bodies. I worked in the hospital at Lake Butler Reception and Medical
Center, tucked within a region littered with prisons in Northeast Florida. One
of the first bodies I wrapped was a man so consumed by depression and
psychosis that he ripped off his own toenail and cut the veins in his elbow
until he bled to death. The smell of congealed, coagulated blood didn't leave
my nostrils; years of therapy won't wash it out. Taking men down after they
hang themselves in confinement, untying the knots, lifting them onto a gurney,
rolling them in plastic, tagging their toe, and placing them in a morgue
freezer, fractures something deep inside my psyche. I watched an old VHS tape
that showed me how to wrap men up like giant tootsie rolls and tag a body. I
was supposedly "educated" in the proper technique and etiquette, but I wasn't
really. An inmate taught me, during the heat of the moment, while a lifeless
corpse stared back at me. "Watch and learn." Talk about a thousand-yard stare.
I soaked it all in. I learned how to close a steel door on another soul and
walk away like it meant nothing. That was my freshman year at crime college.

Death is constant and deliberate. I thought prison was where inmates did their
time, learned a lesson, and then went home. It isn't. It's where people die on
whims. Officers put hits on your head because they think you disrespected
their girlfriend, a nurse, in some infinitesimal way. Inmates die over
jealousy, greed, and ego. Killed, because a renegade guard wants to send a
direct message and gets another inmate to carry it out. That happened to me:
one officer tried to recruit me to kill another inmate he didn't like because
the man might be getting out, was actually innocent, and had a lover visiting
him every weekend. He asked me at the canteen window while I was just trying
to get back to my bunk and read a book, Meanwhile, he was eating honeybuns and
drinking Mountain Dew, casually asking me to murder somebody when I had less
than three years left on my sentence. Murders get written up as suicides and
"medical incidents" because DOC investigates itself. That's the kind of setup
that ought to be hit with the RICO Act. Inside, there are no real checks and
balances. It's the sly fox guarding the henhouse and writing the incident
report when it's really the fox killing the hens.

At Suwannee CI Annex, they threw me in confinement and made sure I knew I was
nothing. They screamed at me to kill myself through the confinement window,
blowing a whistle the whole time. They laughed while they put me on a seventy-
two-hour property strip: no mattress, no clothes, just freezing air, concrete,
boxer shorts, a steel sink, and a steel toilet. Try sleeping like that and
tell me how it goes. They tortured me. They sprayed me with their chemical
agent of choice, "Black Jesus," laughing about how, after they spray a Black
boy with it, it makes him holler for Jesus, his true master. That wasn't
correction. It was racist chemical backed by paperwork that lets it keep going
indefinitely.

I've seen a man struggle to breathe after inhaling chemical agents. That's
just another day at school. Hearing him fight for air was one thing; watching
officers lift him up and slam him onto a steel grated walkway on the second
tier of my confinement wing, right outside my cell door, was another. I heard
the sound of his windpipe crushing. Then the breathing turned to gargles, and
then there was nothing, because he was dead. Knowing officers did the killing
changes everything about what prison really is. This school is death, plain
and simple. It stalked me constantly. It whispered at the edge of my vision.
DOC wants me dead one way or another, inside those walls or after I walk out
through those razor-wire fences.

Guess that was my sophomore year.

Prison is a crime college because it forces you into the ugliest curriculum
just to stay alive. Orientation is confinement. No books, as the officers like
to say, "use your damn imagination, boy." I stared at myself in a tiny, faded,
scratched metal mirror inside the cell and went bonkers. I'd count ten-
thousand steps back and forth across the cold hard floor, lose the number at
six thousand, start over, and do it again. I'd listen to suicide echo down the
wing when a man hung himself and his feet banged against the bunk. That copper
smell hangs in the air when someone slashes their arms with a razorblade. That
metallic stink hits hard and makes every sense in my body light up. Guards
blow their damn whistle, play their terrible "Night Games," and douse men with
the orange mist of Black Jesus. They bang on somebody's window, then stroll
down the tier blaming another man, while the inmate dunks his own T-shirt in
his toilet bowl, desperately wrapping it over his face to keep out the spray,
and scrambles under the bunk, taking shallow breaths through his nostrils,
just his nostrils, or he might choke to death.

On property strip, everything's taken. Imagine a stripped-out closet, white
boxer shorts, a cold steel rack without a mattress, and a steel toilet. In
some places the AC blasts like a punishment of its own; in others, you bake
and swelter in your own sweat. Either way, you're trapped in it. I shivered
for three days and learned the only way to sleep was to do a thousand jumping
jacks just to get my blood moving, then sit on the metal toilet, fold my arms
over my chest like I'm jumping out of a helicopter, tuck my head into my
knees, and steal twenty minutes before the cold catches me again. Once I found
an ant and started talking to her like she was my last friend on earth. I
watched her walk circles and squares across the floor and saved cornbread
crumbs because I figured she was hungry too. I'd headbutt that damn tin mirror
that barely reflected my face and told myself I was a lion, a warrior,
somebody who could handle anything and never break.

Screw this.

Damn these officers.

And anyone who thinks they can break me.

You've got to choose who you're going to be from the get-go, or you get swept
up into the crime college, where the lessons make strong mothers weep.

At Taylor Correctional Institution, crime college turns into advanced
seminars. The dorm goes dark at lights out. K-2 smoke hangs in the air. Guys
bug out on spice and think they're snakes or talk to the devil. Men strap up.
They tie magazines to their ribs with plastic wrap, wrap their arms with
blankets and sheets, and lace their shoes tight, because there's nothing worse
than being caught in socks when the knives come out and rubber soles are the
only chance you've got. Swords get bent off cooking racks in the chow hall
bathroom, broken back and forth until the metal fractures, then smuggled to
the dorm and sharpened for hours on concrete, and the back-and-forth grinding
sound becomes the prison's lullaby. Shanks get carved from fence wire and
Plexiglas. Razors handed out for shaving turn into weapons. Locks swing in
canteen bags or hang off belts to smash whoever's in front of you.

Most dorm riots are more about fear and control than murder. Most guys aren't
trained assassins. They're scared men trying not to die. To kill somebody,
you've got to be fully committed, and most aren't. That's why I saw more blood
and stitches than toe tags during riots. But one-on-one, when there's real
beef or a guard wants someone gone, the danger spikes and the curriculum gets
more advanced. Every time a dorm erupts, the lights flip on and off, the
intercom screams "Back to your bunks," and everybody starts scrambling to hide
weapons in vents and walls, washing blood from under their fingernails with
bottled water, putting on that clueless, lifeless mask for the search teams
when they enter the dorm. I stood naked on slippery wet tile while officers
barked their orders: arms up, mouth open, tongue out, turn around, spread your
ass cheeks, squat and cough, one foot up, other foot. Then we were herded into
a hot dayroom with a hundred and twenty other men, pressed against the wall,
wondering if the knife hidden over my bunk by my gang-member bunkee was about
to end up in my face when a sergeant demanded to know if I was in a gang.

Yeah, that happened.

That's what most people call "doing time": eight and a half years of advanced
riot practice, knife practice, survival practice, and sitting on bunks
watching TV. Nobody's talking about real mental health care. Nobody's talking
about house arrest with structure. It's ten years of mayhem and then, if
you're lucky, a bus ride home with a head full of shit you never had a chance
to process.

Some of my professors at crime college were inmates. Some were officers.

At Lake Butler, the hospital walls used to say, "Browns Stick Together," a
reminder that brown-shirt officers protect each other first and last. Their
oath doesn't even mention prisoners. It pledges loyalty to fellow officers,
superiors, and the institution. The people they're supposed to correct don't
exist anywhere in it. That's the lesson they hand out, ruler in hand, striking
anyone who misbehaves.

Prison seems hopeless and a complete waste of time if correction is the true
aim. You walk out more wrecked than you went in. For me, it became a war zone
I chose to turn into a classroom. And don't get me started on the monotony,
the waiting around, the endless question of what's going to pop off next. Half
the time there's literally nothing to do. It's all on you to decide who you
want to be and what you're about. Where's the real guidance.

Junior year.

Florida DOC's slogan is "We Never Walk Alone." On the outside it sounds like
teamwork. Inside it reads like gang writing. It means the most powerful crew
in the system doesn't wear colors. They wear badges. It means when a guard
beats you, sprays you, kills you, writes you up, ships you across the state,
or hides you in confinement, there's usually a good old boy network behind him
smoothing paperwork and closing ranks. A few years back, three Florida prison
guards were arrested as active members of the Ku Klux Klan for plotting to
murder a formerly incarcerated Black man, and I knew one of those officers,
personally. They wanted to stage it as a medical emergency and place a fishing
pole in his hands while he was just trying to catch a meal in the St. Johns
River. That case made the news, but plenty of plots don't. The names change.
The culture doesn't.

There was Officer Jerk, weather-beaten, pushing fifty, with the murderous
intelligence of a kid burning ants with a magnifying glass. He'd line us up
and ask, "Who's a pedophile on this wing." Whoever got pointed out had to say
the age of his victim. Under twelve. Under six. That's more than enough.
Jerk's slap would drop the first man, urine soaking his pants, blood coming
out his mouth and ears. Then Sergeant Dread, known on the compound for killing
people with one open palm once he slipped on black leather gloves, would go
looking for a second-class project. I'd see him slap a person so hard I knew
the administration would have to make up a story, like an English assignment
at school. First the seizure, then the fall. Anything but the truth. Inside
Lake Butler and other camps, inmates are in gangs, but so are certain
officers, and their gang has all the real power.

Senior year.

Then there was Officer Colon. Puerto Rican. Skinny. Rat-faced. He acted like
every woman on the compound wanted him. The kind of man who liked to have an
inmate cuffed behind his back before he starts punching, who loved spraying
defenseless men with chemicals, setting up guys he doesn't like with knives or
drugs, and getting off on watching people suffer. He had a girlfriend, Miss
Piggy, who ratted out my friend Kennedy's relationship with Nurse Marie.
Kennedy wasn't hustling Marie. It was mutual respect and love, one thing
prison is supposed to erase. Piggy's jealousy got Kennedy fired and beaten.
After that Colon turned his eyes on me. Flaco brought the message: "You're
dead, Tatter."

When guys on the pound told me Colon had put a contract hit on me, two ounces
and a phone on my life, they said no. In a place where people will kill you
for less, turning down that kind of payment is love. It doesn't change the
math. "Just because we didn't take it," they said, "doesn't mean another dude
won't." What a math lesson this school's providing. I made a Plexiglas knife,
taped it to my leg under my blues, weighed down by it like I had Frodo's ring,
walked into the psych ward ready to make it him or me. My mom already knew the
plan. If I hadn't called by six-thirty, she'd be calling administration,
calling Tallahassee, doing anything she could to stop the coverup. Colon sat
in his chair, boots on the desk, three officers around him, tapping a pen like
he was controlling the room with sound while my fingers inched toward the
knife. After my speech I prepared, he dropped his chair with a bang, slammed
the pen down and said, "Okay, Tatter. It's dead. Don't you never walk down
that hall while she's working unless you're escorted by another officer." The
hit was cancelled. Knife unused, thankfully. Just another day at work.

That's what mercy looks like in this college.

For almost everybody around me, prison was a complete waste of time. For me,
it became a war zone I chose to turn into a classroom. Inside that crime
college, I started the first inmate-led yoga program in the Florida DOC. I
designed classes so men could work through trauma and heal their bodies and
hearts. I studied Spanish and practiced skits with friends. I read every book
I could get my hands on and used those books as mentors, leaning on them for
support and inspiration. If they were going to cage my body, I was going to
free my mind.

Arturo Pérez-Reverte's books gave me history, honor codes, values, and morals
to stand upon. David Benioff's City of Thieves showed me how bad things can
get and still leave room for humor and humanity. Unbroken gave me courage when
I felt literally broken from food poisoning, forced to spend hour after hour
in confinement while officers decided whether I was faking or high on K-2,
fluids draining out of every part of me, and still wanted me working the next
day at the front gate. "This too shall pass" became my mantra. I adopted
survival as a mission; live, make it back home to my family and loved ones.
Our families serve hard time too. They're hostages of DOC right alongside us.
Every missed birthday. Every canceled visit. Every phone call that costs way
too much. My mom drove to see me, sent books, showed up for me the day I got
out, and fought for me when my brain broke. She did a ten-year sentence in her
own way, and then more on the outside dealing with my flashbacks and probation
bullshit. When we talk about "public safety" and "correction," we never factor
in the mothers, fathers, and kids, chained to those prison timelines. They're
paying for this crime college just as much as we are.

And college is expensive.

All this might be okay if prison actually provided rehabilitation and support
afterward. It doesn't. Prison doesn't heal trauma. It multiplies it by some
crazy amount. It does nothing to fix behavior that community alternatives and
mental health care couldn't handle more humanely, more safely, and far
cheaper. It's a big, expensive revolving door of recidivism, and then they
point to that revolving door as an excuse to build more prisons.

I went for another degree after graduation.

My brain finally short-circuited in January 2021, after I'd been back in
society since August 2018. I wasn't on drugs. I was on years of institutional
warfare. I fought multiple guards, unfortunately, and got shocked more than
half a dozen times with tasers. I woke up in a hospital bed with a broken
face, orbital fractures, stitches, and two black eyes. Then they dragged me to
a suicide cell in a turtle suit on battery, on law-enforcement charges. The
system calls that correction, but it was a real breakdown built out of trauma
and lack of sleep, taught by the state and then ignored.

Dude has it summed up right, I'd say. A year of mental health care or
structured house arrest does what steel doors, concrete walls, and razor
fences never will. My real rehabilitation didn't happen within the belly of
the beast. It happened because, the minute I bonded out, my mom drove me
straight to Epic Behavioral Healthcare in St. Augustine. I showed up every
week, sometimes twice a week, for two years. I got properly diagnosed with
complex PTSD. I learned how to breathe again, started my yoga practice again,
and finished my memoir, COUNT TIME. After a brutal year fighting for my
freedom, the court gave me six months of house arrest and five years of
probation, with a mountain of fees waiting to bleed my wallet dry. Those six
months of house arrest, tied with Epic Behavioral Healthcare and actual
structure, did more for public safety than ten years inside ever did. I was
with my family and loved ones, I knew I'd messed up, and even then, I wanted
something different from the life I was living. I wasn't happy. I was lost. As
I focused on self-improvement, my determination kept growing. I promised
myself I'd commit to changing my life and do whatever was necessary to make
myself and my family proud.

None of that came from DOC. Please call prison what it really is, or what it
should be called: state-sponsored human trafficking and a mass-incarceration
nightmare. Every contract is built on our bodies and a massive amount of sweat
equity. Phones, emails, video visits, money transfers, commissary, food,
medical care, laundry, PRIDE labor, private prisons, and each time a family
sends a dollar, somebody gets rich. Every time a man picks up trash on the
side of the road or sews a uniform, somebody sells the product at full price
while he earns pennies or nothing. In Florida, we earned zilch unless we were
fortunate enough to land a job at PRIDE. Follow the money from every prison
contract, every JPay transaction, every commissary markup, every food invoice,
every medical payment, every phone fee, every money transfer cut, every bond
that builds a new facility, every dollar of inmate labor that goes into a
product, and you end up in one place: state capital. The people who'd have to
authorize a real investigation are the same people whose names are already on
the contracts. The mob would be impressed. I know they would. The paperwork,
the silence, the insulation from accountability. It's a rigged network
engineered to be untouchable.

Even letters are part of the warehouse scam now. Physical mail's banned. Every
birthday card, kid's drawing, and family photo gets intercepted, scanned by a
for-profit contractor, and delivered as a digital file on a tablet, and
families can't even send stamps anymore, which were a form of currency and a
way to write about what really happens inside prison walls between a daughter
and a dad, a son and a mom, grandparents, aunties and uncles, friends, and
lovers. They say it's "contraband reduction," but states that tried the same
thing saw overdoses go up, not down. Cutting off real mail isn't about safety,
hell no, it's strictly about control and erasure. It's about making a person
disappear while he's still breathing and charging enormous fees every step of
the way, and it makes me sick.

Go watch The Alabama Solution on HBO Max or rent it on Apple TV and sit with
it. That's really happening in prisons. I know it is in Florida, too. All the
killing, corruption, and human farming. Alabama, Florida, all these states are
generating tons of cash by trapping people, renting out their labor, skimming
their wages or not paying them at all, and calling it, ta-daa, "justice."

Florida's the worst system I know, but these stories aren't unique. They move
across states like franchises with different logos but the same lucrative
business model.

Grrrrrrr.

Inside Taylor CI, I watched a man die, struck with locks again and again by
four guys while two more stabbed him, less than twenty-five yards from the
dorm. I watched young guys like Sam come in with thirteen months and turn into
targets. Sam looked white but was Latino. A predator with life was already
sizing him up. Then, at master count, an officer walked in calling count time
and stopped at Sam's bunk, then made poor Sam walk the dorm, sashaying his
hips, flicking his wrist, saying "whoops, did I do that" around the perimeter
of the dorm like freaking Urkel until count cleared. If Sam wasn't a target
before, he was after that.

School's in session.

Another day, a sergeant thought an inmate had told on her, and she walked that
man into every dorm on the compound, more than a thousand men, and announced
he was a snitch and a "chump-bitch." That's a conscripted death sentence. The
man was beaten so badly you couldn't recognize him. That's crime college.
That's our lesson from the judicial system. I learned what one sentence from a
guard can do to my life, and it was a real eye-opener.

I'm not pretending everyone's innocent. I know dudes who'd literally eat your
face and then eat the fruit cocktail at chow and not think twice about it.
Flesh eaters exist. Child rapists exist. Predators exist. But most of us
aren't that. Most people inside made a series of terrible choices inside
systems of poverty, racism, hate, addiction, and a legal structure where a
halfway decent defense costs more than a family will ever be able to afford.
Plenty of people caught in the jaws of the legal world are forced to let a
judge decide their fate while the District Attorney hangs a crazy amount of
time over their head. They plead guilty and pray the person on the bench won't
railroad them and send them into a den of thieves, rapists, liars, and
killers, where the real predators are built into a predatory system that locks
you up, throws away the key, and uses our bodies as punching bags.

Chief Judge Pamela L. North told me that if I'd caught these charges in
Maryland, I never would have served a ten-year mandatory sentence. That shook
me. What is justice? Who is it truly for? What does it really mean when the
same crime in a different zip code doesn't bury a young man for a decade. It
isn't some clean, universal idea. It's a map of power, politics, and profit.
And I was stuck on the wrong part of the crumpled-up map.

Dr. Kelly Vannan's trash can slide during a Lifelong Learning Institute
lecture at Flagler College I helped co-lead says it all. She told the room
that's what society thinks of us, that we're trash. She said that once we are
sent to prison and the doors slam behind us, that nobody thinks about the
trash once it's thrown out. When I spoke, I put that trash can back up on the
screen and said this: the mob looked at trash and turned it into a
multibillion-dollar business. That's exactly what our government, the DOC,
corporate shareholders, and executives think about. They look at the
incarcerated and see money. They're banking on the public not thinking about
any of us because silence breeds profit. Mass incarceration is a for-profit
epidemic. It's a corporate warehouse program where private contracts, bed
quotas, and slave labor are dressed up as public safety. From Jim Crow
attitudes in administration to modern slave labor on production lines, the
incentives all point the same way: lock us away, sign more contracts, and
extract a shitload more cash.

I guess now I'm part of the Lifelong Learning Institute college program after
the education prison taught me.

I'm not the only one saying this. The Marshall Project ran Joey Heilman's
essay, "I Spent 78 Days in a Violent Youth Jail. I Have PTSD For Life."
Seventy-eight days. Barely three months, and I'm not taking that away from him
in the least. Twenty-two years later he's still screaming in his car, still
snapping back to beatdowns in the dark, still feeling his nervous system flip
into survival mode at his kid's school picnic. Less than one summer in a
juvenile cage and his mind's wired for flashbacks, fright, and panic. So what
do you think a ten-year mandatory sentence in maximum-security adult complexes
does? What about twenty years, or thirty, or seventy-eight days? What do you
think wrapping bodies and dodging hits and watching officers kill people does
to a person? It's sure not "correction."

It's structural damage. It programs people like robots to mess up.

Without real help, all most people ever really do is stare at walls and bars,
surrounded by wild shit, and call that "doing time." What guidance is there in
that? You're stripped bare of identity and reduced to a number, an inmate, and
a body in a crummy, uncomfortable bed. It takes a real solid mind and a shit-
ton of stubbornness not to get swept up in the DOC shitstorm, into the
boredom, the violence, the dehumanization, and the slow grind that eats your
soul.

When you walk out, your sentence isn't over. Every flashback adds more time.
Every panic attack adds a few more minutes to your stay in college.
Rehabilitation after prison should be the system's priority, but it isn't. The
Department of Corrections is not trying to heal anybody. They want you as
broken, desensitized, and scared as possible. They want every mistake to drive
up the recidivism tally and give them another excuse to play "Captain
America," posing like heroes in front of a razor-wire backdrop while cashing
in their dirty prison poker chips for cold hard cash.

Courtrooms aren't built to find truth. They're stages where conflicting
stories compete. Real defense costs a fortune, and innocent people go down
every day just to fit a prosecutor's narrative. People get sentenced to death
who are completely innocent. In this setup, it isn't about what happened. It's
about what you can prove, and whichever story wins becomes the decree. If you
can't afford a story that beats the state, you lose your life. That's the
game. That's crime college inside, story war outside, and warehouse profit on
top.

Here's the part DOC never wants you to see. Former criminal defense attorney
and retired Chief Circuit Court Judge Pamela L. North read my memoir, Count
Time, and provided this blurb: "No more proof is needed that behind prison
walls lies abundant untapped talent than this riveting account of prison life
by Emmett Tatter. Far from portraying himself as a saint, Tatter provides us
with a truthful description of his time inside, revealing questionable
morality at times, also known as human behavior. All told in the most colorful
and graphic manner."

That's a judge who's seen thousands of cases, telling you straight that behind
prison walls lies "abundant" untapped talent. We aren't trash, nor villains,
and not all of us are beastly monsters. We are human beings, screwed up and
flawed, with questionable morality like every person walking the streets, but
still capable of telling the truth in living color and changing our lives.
That's the heart of this. DOC isn't a superhero. It's not the brave guardian
in some comic book. It's a worldwide syndicate in a flashy costume sporting a
damn cape. It warehouses human beings, erases their gifts, bleeds them of
everything, and then sells you the story that it's saving the day.

What a hero.

Learning this is how you truly graduate from the prison system's colleges.

Not everyone outside is blind. PEN America believes in incarcerated writers
and lets us put our stories on paper. Reginald Dwayne Betts went from solitary
to Yale Law and built Freedom Libraries because he knows books save lives.
Shaka Senghor, Ian Manuel, Keri Blakinger, and a whole army of people turned
years inside into work that helps instead of destroys. My life is part of that
same ecosystem. Les Standiford, a New York Times bestselling author and
founding director of the Florida International University Creative Writing
Program, called Count Time searing and unforgettable. Dr. Baz Dreisinger,
author of Incarceration Nations, justice worker, professor at John Jay
College, and founder of the Prison-to-College Pipeline, said my voice is a
warning the world needs to heed "now more than ever." John DeDakis, an award-
winning journalist, former senior copy editor on CNN's The Situation Room with
Wolf Blitzer, and mystery-suspense novelist, called my story a raw, wrenching
argument for prison reform and self-reform. Professors who support my work,
Kelly Vannan, Kim Bradley, Mandy Miller, and Allan Marcil, all saw the same
thing: behind the mugshot and DOC number, there's a real face staring back at
you.

And it's me looking at you, and you looking back at me, at eye level.

My life proves the stigma's bullshit. The only things that ever changed anyone
I knew inside were the things the state tried to keep out: books, education,
yoga, real mental health care, and real connection. My first love was reading,
and books mentored me when nothing else could. That's why Freedom Libraries
matter. That's why PEN America matters. That's why inmate-led yoga classes
matter. Real journalism matters. On one rec yard, we stood on prison grass and
learned how to breathe together, and it helped. It changed our bodies and
minds. It gave men something besides violence to show up for. It instilled
real passion, the passion to be better and to become resilient against the
clutches of the DOC dream snatcher.

We don't need more prisons. We need community mental health clinics on the
front end of crime. We need house arrest and ankle monitors tied to therapy,
classes, and work instead of warehousing people in concrete boxes. We need
Freedom Libraries and PEN America style writing programs in every jail and
prison so that once a person falls in love with letters and the books they
read, they've got another way to live and a real chance in the free world. A
chance to dream. We need inmate-built yoga and trauma recovery in every dorm,
not just on one yard or in a couple of classrooms where some crazy convict,
me, decided to teach downward dog. We need real reentry on the back end:
housing, jobs, union-backed training, ongoing therapy, mentors, and someone
who believes in you, the stuff the system pretends is optional. We also need
to take the first step and choose to be different. We must decide to change,
and with real programs and someone telling you that you're something other
than a piece of shit convict, it makes your chances a hell of a lot better.

Build that, and prison stops becoming the first answer. The crime college is
closed. Warehouse programs shrink, people heal instead of rot, and the state
stops using bodies as sweat equity and starts treating them like actual human
beings. It stops killing us and making our loved ones cry. Then you finally
start living in a country where "public safety" means safety, not profit.

That question made me want to answer it. This is it. For most men I lived
with, prison was ten years of staring at walls and learning how to survive
violence. For me, it was redemption, and I refused to let hell own my story. I
turned that college into my classroom for revolution. Yoga classes. Spanish
skits in the dorm. Books stacked on the bunk. Therapy when I got out. I'm
living proof that if we give people real tools instead of crap, they can make
their time count instead of letting the big house count them as trash.

Until that happens, prison keeps winning. Look at recidivism and look at all
the death counts inside the almost 1,700 prisons, and that's just prisons, not
county jails. Look at overdose and suicide after release. Vegas doesn't have
shit on DOC. You walk into prison and the odds are stacked against your soul.
You walk out, and DOC is standing there with open jaws, waiting for you to
stumble so it can swallow you whole again.

Do this. Watch The Alabama Solution. Let the killing, corruption, and slave
labor sink in. Then look back at everything I've told you here about Florida's
prisons, about crime college, about the warehouse program, about untapped
talent wasting away behind a system that doesn't give a damn.

Now be honest and ask yourself one final question.

The superhero with state-sponsored crime colleges popping up all over this
country like poisonous mushrooms isn't saving us.

So, who are the real gangsters?

And who the hell's paying their salary.

Maybe the superhero you've been cheering for is just the gangster in costume,
or suit.
